title: Constantine
hook: an emperor sees a sign before battle, and everything changes for the church, for good and ill

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antony, and your line was he heard, and went. What did you give away? Day seven hundred sixty-six.

For days now, the people in this story have been on the wrong side of power. A letter explaining Christians to outsiders. Justin writing to the emperor. Perpetua in the arena. Tertullian daring the governors. Cyprian's people nursing the sick in a frightened city. Today the camera turns around. A Roman ruler named Constantine is marching on Rome to fight a rival for the empire. And before the battle, by his own account, he sees something in the sky. He is not a Christian. He is about to become a very powerful friend to the church, and that changes the story.

We have two old accounts, and they don't match exactly. Eusebius, a bishop who knew Constantine, writes that the emperor himself told him, and swore to it, that around noon he saw a cross of light above the sun, with words: by this, conquer. That night, Eusebius says, Christ appeared to him in a dream and told him to make a copy of the sign and carry it into battle. So Constantine had a standard made with the first two Greek letters of Christ's name. Another writer of the time, Lactantius, tells it more simply: in a dream, Constantine was told to mark the heavenly sign of God on his soldiers' shields, and he did. A vision in the sky, or a dream, or both. The sources differ, and that's worth saying plainly. What happened next is that Constantine won, and he favored the church. Christians who had been hunted now found their emperor on their side. Their buildings could rise in public. Their bishops could meet openly. And there's the other side. When the emperor is your friend, the emperor has opinions about your church. Faith and power start to tangle in ways Christians have argued about since. Jesus had said, "My kingdom is not of this world." Now a kingdom of this world was carrying his sign into battle. Christians still weigh this differently. Some see Constantine as God's answer to the prayers of the persecuted, and the Orthodox Church honors him as a saint. Others see the moment the church began to trade the arena for the palace, and wonder what that cost. Some hold both at once. Eusebius adds one more detail. Constantine was baptized only near the end of his life.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about faith and power. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place where you hold a little power: at work, at home, in a group, over someone younger or newer than you. Then ask two quiet questions. What does what I believe, about God or about people, ask of me there? And where might the power be shaping the belief, instead of the other way around? Don't rush to an answer. If you pray, you can bring that place before God. If you don't, simply look at it honestly for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Constantine. The emperor who said he saw a sign before battle, and who turned the church from hunted to favored, for good and ill.
Your line: power changes things. Today, in the place you named, use your bit of power once on behalf of someone with less. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: The Orthodox Church honors Constantine as a saint, together with his mother Helena; other Christians remember him as a pivotal and debated figure in the church's history with the state.

myth: the old sources agree exactly on what Constantine saw
Eusebius tells of a cross of light in the sky and a dream; Lactantius tells only of a dream.
Eusebius says Constantine was baptized only near the end of his life
he favored the church long before he was baptized.
the Latin words in hoc signo vinces are what Eusebius wrote
Eusebius wrote in Greek: touto nika, by this conquer. the Latin form is a later wording.

fork.setup: you're a bishop. the emperor who once would have killed you now wants to be your friend, build your churches and attend your meetings. what do you do?
options: welcome it: the persecution is over.
refuse: the church must stay away from power.
welcome it, and worry about what it will cost.
fork.reveal: the church welcomed Constantine's favor, and Christians still argue about what it cost. both the relief and the worry are part of the story.

original.note: Greek: by this, conquer. the words Eusebius says Constantine saw with the sign.

trapdoor: what you thought: Constantine became a Christian and everything got better.
what it means: an emperor's sign before battle turned the church from hunted to favored, and tangled faith with power.
what a scholar hears: two accounts, Eusebius's cross of light and Lactantius's dream, that don't match; and a baptism Eusebius places near the end of his life.

notes: The index says 'in 312'; the script states no date (the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, against Maxentius, is not named). Confirm.

Eusebius, Life 1.28–31: cross of light above the sun, 'τούτῳ νίκα', Christ in a dream, the labarum with chi-rho. Lactantius, Deaths of the Persecutors 44: dream, heavenly sign on shields. Paraphrased; confirm.
'Orthodox Christians honor him as a saint' (with Helena, 'equal to the apostles'); confirm. The two readings of Constantine are presented without ranking.
Baptism near death: Life of Constantine 4.61–62. Confirm.
Myth 3: the Latin 'in hoc signo vinces' as a later form; confirm.

Editor pass: Constantine is called a ruler, not a general (he already held imperial rank when he marched on Rome); 'Orthodox Christians honor him' now names the Orthodox Church rather than all its members.
